Why & what to watch

Why this is the next step

With a steady pour, a little more yield can lift extraction and soften sharp sourness. Expect a slightly lighter body.

Keep steady

Dose, grind, temperature, and pre-infusion. Taste before changing anything else.

What to look for

Look for sweetness and a softer finish. If the extra yield only thins the shot, return to your previous yield and try a small grind adjustment.

Temperature for this roast

A starting range for medium roasts is 91–94 °C.

Recipe notes & sources

How to use this guide: the decision map is an app interpretation, not a verbatim video recipe. Yield targets use a trial change of 10%; this is not a rule from either video. Taste the result before making another change.

James Hoffmann on espresso temperature · James Hoffmann on shot time · La Marzocco’s brew guide

Under 20 s and over 40 s are rough cues for a conventional shot. If you use a long pre-infusion or a different brew ratio, choose the flow you observed.

Start with a repeatable shot

Check headspace with the dry, tamped puck: insert and remove the portafilter without brewing. If the shower screen or screw leaves a mark, reduce the dose. Basket ratings are a starting point; coffee density changes the space occupied.

  1. Fit the dose to the basket. Start near the basket’s rated dose and leave room above the tamped puck. Weigh the grounds, distribute evenly, and tamp level. Keep the dose fixed for the first comparisons.
  2. Weigh the yield. A useful first try is 1:2 by mass, such as 18 g dry coffee to 36 g espresso. Put a scale under the cup and stop by weight. A longer ratio usually gives higher extraction and lower concentration.
  3. Use grind to get a steady flow. A smaller grind step is usually enough. Finer generally slows the shot, coarser speeds it up. If finer makes the flow uneven or the finish drying, back off and check puck prep.
  4. Taste, then log. Stir and taste after it cools a little. Around 30 s is a starting reference for a conventional shot. Record total time from pump or lever start and the pre-infusion time separately. Keep a balanced shot even when its time differs.

Pre-infusion

Flair’s guide ↗
Dark roast
About 3–5 s at 2–3 bar as a short-soak trial.
Medium roast
About 5–8 s at 2–3 bar as a starting comparison.
Light roast
About 8–15 s at 1–2 bar if a gentler, longer soak helps.

These are Flair-style trial ranges. With adjustable pre-infusion, compare shots about 2–3 s apart at the same pressure, dose, grind, yield, and temperature. If your machine has a fixed program, keep it and work on grind or yield. As soon as you see a stream, some of your yield is already in the cup.

Read the cup

Acidity is not automatically a defect, especially in light roasts. Keep a recipe you enjoy. Taste and flow suggest experiments, not a certain diagnosis; coffee, water, preparation and equipment also matter.

Sour, bitter, and dry feel different

Sharp, mouthwatering acidity can point to low extraction, especially with fast flow. Bitterness lingers like unsweetened cocoa or burnt toast. Astringency feels drying, like oversteeped tea. Sour and drying together, early spurts, or big shot-to-shot swings are reasons to check distribution and flow first.

Try a little extra yield in a separate cup

At your usual target weight, swap in a second cup for a few more grams. Taste the base shot, then add a little of the extra liquid back. If the acidity softens and sweetness improves, try a slightly higher target on the next shot.

Temperature and pressure come later

Once grind and yield are repeatable, try a small temperature increase for a light roast that stays sharp. Cooler water can help a dark roast that tastes harsh. Keep your machine’s usual pressure while learning. If it supports profiling, try a gentler ramp once you have a repeatable shot.

Hoffmann’s light-roast example

His first shot was slow and tasted muddy and sour. He went coarser, then made smaller steps finer after overshooting. Once the flow and taste improved, he kept the grind steady and raised the yield from about 38 g to 42 g from an 18 g dose. The shot lost some body and gained sweetness. Later, he reduced the dose to about 17 g, ground finer again, and kept the 42 g yield for that coffee.
